title: Power with a word and a touch
sum: Jesus comes down from the mountain where he taught (chapters 5–7) and now acts. A man with a skin disease asks to be made clean, and Jesus touches him. A Gentile centurion asks for his servant and believes that a word from Jesus is enough, and Jesus says he has not met such faith in Israel. Peter's mother-in-law is healed and gets up to serve him, and at evening crowds of sick and possessed people are brought. Matthew sees in all this the Servant of Isaiah 53:4, who "took our weaknesses and carried our diseases."

The second half asks what it costs to follow such a Lord. A scribe and a disciple hear hard sayings about homelessness and the dead burying their dead. Then the disciples follow him into a boat, a storm shakes the sea, and Jesus calms it with a word. On the far shore, in Gentile country, two men with demons meet him; the demons go into a herd of pigs, and the town asks Jesus to leave. Authority over sickness, nature and the spirit world is on display, but so are fear, little faith and rejection.
readings: The stories fit Galilee under Herod Antipas: a lakeside town with a toll station and an officer of the ruler's army, fishing families, boats on a lake known for sudden storms, Greek cities on the far shore that raised pigs. Historians of Jesus, Jewish and Christian alike, agree that he was known as a healer and exorcist; even hostile sources later called him a sorcerer. Matthew retells stories also found in Mark and Luke, usually shorter and with the focus on Jesus' words and the people's faith.
Read as a story about authority

The Sermon ended with the crowds astonished that Jesus taught "as one who held authority" (7:29). Chapter 8 shows that authority at work. The centurion, himself a man under authority, sees it clearly: Jesus need only speak. His word cleanses, heals at a distance, drives out spirits and stills the sea. The men in the boat ask the chapter's question: "What sort of person is this?"
Read as a picture of discipleship

Between the miracles stand sayings on following (8:18–22), and the storm story begins with the disciples "following" him into the boat. Many readers, ancient and modern, see the boat as the church: following Jesus brings no shelter from storms, but he is in the boat, and the right cry is "Lord, save us!"

views.H: Capernaum lay in the territory of Herod Antipas, near the border with his brother Philip's land and across the lake from the Greek cities of the Decapolis. The centurion probably served Antipas. Healers and exorcists were known in Judaism (Josephus tells of an exorcist named Eleazar before Vespasian, Jewish Antiquities 8.46–49), and the historian's question is less whether Jesus was known for such deeds than how they were understood.
views.C: Matthew follows Mark's order only loosely here. He gathers miracle stories from Mark 1, 4 and 5 and adds the centurion from the material he shares with Luke (often called Q). He shortens them, often by half, cutting vivid details to sharpen the dialogue and the theme of faith, as Heinz Joachim Held showed. Two demoniacs instead of one, and a fulfillment quotation (8:17), are his own touches.
views.L: Chapters 8–9 are framed by the summaries of 4:23 and 9:35 and hold ten miracles in three groups, with sayings between: three healings (8:1–17), sayings on discipleship (8:18–22), three acts of power (8:23–9:8), the call of Matthew and the question of fasting (9:9–17), three or four healings (9:18–34). After the words of the new Moses come his works.
views.J: A Jewish reader notices how Jewish the stories are: Jesus sends the healed man to the priest as the Torah requires, and he wears tassels (9:20). The saying about many coming from east and west (8:11–12) draws on prophetic hopes for the gathering of exiles and nations. Later Christian use of 8:12 to say that Jews are cast out is a reading many churches now reject; within Matthew the same warning is aimed at his own church (13:38–42; 22:11–14).
views.T: The church fathers loved this chapter. Chrysostom and Augustine held up the centurion's humility, and his words became part of the Communion liturgy in East and West. The storm became a favorite image of the church as a ship (Tertullian), and 8:17 was read with Isaiah 53 as showing that Christ's work heals body and soul.

deep.b:
Matthew sets his first collection of miracles right after the Sermon on the Mount, framed by two almost identical summaries (4:23; 9:35). Inside are ten miracles in three groups, separated by sayings:

  • Three healings (8:1–17): a man with skin disease, a centurion's servant, Peter's mother-in-law. Each is someone on the edge: an unclean man, a Gentile, a woman. The section ends with Isaiah 53:4.
  • Interlude on following (8:18–22): a scribe and a disciple.
  • Three acts of power (8:23–9:8): over the sea, over demons, over sin and paralysis.
  • Interlude on the new (9:9–17): the call of a tax collector, a meal with sinners, a question about fasting.
  • Three (or four) restorations (9:18–34): a dead girl and a bleeding woman, two blind men, a man who could not speak.

The answer of the crowds, "Never has anything like this appeared in Israel" (9:33), and the Pharisees' charge (9:34) close the set. In chapter 10 Jesus hands this same authority to the Twelve (10:1, 8).

Compare the man with demons: Mark 5:1–20 runs to 20 verses, Matthew's to 7 (8:28–34). Matthew leaves out the chains, the name Legion, the number of pigs, and the healed man's wish to follow Jesus. The same happens with the paralyzed man (no roof dug through) and the official's daughter (no messengers, no name). In a classic study Heinz Joachim Held argued that Matthew retells miracles like a teacher: he trims the scenery and keeps the conversation, so that each story teaches about faith, discipleship or who Jesus is. That is why so many of Matthew's miracle stories turn on a short exchange: "if you want to" and "I want to"; "only say a word"; "Lord, save us"; "Do you believe I can do this?"

deep.h: Gadara, Gerasa, Gergesa: where did it happen?
deep.b: The manuscripts of all three Gospels disagree about the name of the place (see the variant at 8:28). In the oldest copies Mark and Luke say "the land of the Gerasenes" and Matthew "the land of the Gadarenes." Gerasa, today's Jerash in Jordan, is more than thirty miles from the lake, too far for pigs to run into it. Gadara, today's Umm Qais, stood about six miles from the lake, and its territory reached the shore; coins of Gadara even show a ship. Origen, writing about AD 240, said a town called Gergesa stood on the lake by a steep bank, and that local people pointed out the place. A Byzantine monastery and chapel at Kursi, on the eastern shore below a steep slope, has long been linked with the story. Most scholars think Matthew, who knew the geography, changed Mark's "Gerasenes" to the nearer and better-known Gadara.

settings.what: The cleansing of a man with skin disease, and Jesus' order to show himself to the priest
settings.to: Jesus; then the healed man, with the crowds from the Sermon on the Mount nearby
settings.when: as Jesus comes down the mountain after the Sermon (8:1)
settings.why: The man asks to be made clean, trusting Jesus' power but unsure of his will. Jesus answers both. His order applies the law of Leviticus 13–14, which bound every Israelite declared clean of skin disease: he must be inspected by a priest and bring offerings at the Temple in Jerusalem before rejoining the community. Jesus does not replace the priests; he sends the man to them. Knowing this, the scene reads as obedience to the Torah, not a challenge to it.
settings.readers: For Matthew's Jewish-Christian readers, this first deed after the Sermon shows Jesus doing what he said in 5:17: fulfilling the Law, not abolishing it.

settings.what: The centurion's request, and Jesus' sayings on faith and the great banquet
settings.to: Jesus; then (8:10–12) "the people following him," a mostly Jewish crowd in Capernaum
settings.when: as Jesus enters Capernaum
settings.why: The officer, probably a Gentile in Herod Antipas's service, asks help for his servant but will not ask Jesus to enter a Gentile house. Jesus' words to the crowd turn his faith into a warning: outsiders will sit at Abraham's table, and those who assume a place may lose it. The words were meant to shake the confidence of hearers who took the kingdom for granted.
settings.readers: Matthew's community, Jewish believers now welcoming Gentiles, could see their own mixed table foreshadowed, and hear a warning against presuming on their own standing (compare 22:11–14).
views: Jesus speaks 8:11–12 to the crowd after praising a Gentile; the "many" are Gentiles (most interpreters).
Luke puts the saying in a different scene, on the road to Jerusalem, answering a question about how many will be saved (Luke 13:23–30); many think it circulated on its own and each Gospel placed it.
Davies and Allison argue the saying originally meant Jews scattered abroad coming home to the feast.

settings.what: Two sayings on following Jesus
settings.to: a scribe who offers to follow him, and a man already counted among his disciples
settings.when: as Jesus gives the order to cross the lake, with crowds pressing around
settings.why: To spell out the cost of following before the boat leaves: no settled home, and a claim that outranks even the duty to bury a father. The sayings test whether the volunteers understand what they are offering.
settings.readers: Matthew's church still sent out wandering preachers who left homes and families (10:9–14); these sayings described their life, and asked settled believers to keep the same priorities.

settings.what: Jesus' rebuke in the storm
settings.to: the disciples in the boat
settings.when: after they wake him, with the boat in danger of sinking
settings.why: He speaks to their fear before he speaks to the storm, naming their "little faith" so they will learn to trust him in danger.
settings.readers: Early Christians facing persecution read the scene as their own: the church in a storm, with the Lord present (Bornkamm).

settings.what: The demons' cry and Jesus' one-word command
settings.by: the demons, speaking through the two men; then Jesus
settings.to: Jesus; then the demons
settings.when: on the far shore, in Gentile country near Gadara, among the tombs
settings.why: The demons recognize Jesus as "Son of God" before any disciple does, and fear that their judgment has come "ahead of time." They bargain to be sent into the pigs. Jesus answers with a single word, "Go!", showing that his authority reaches beyond Israel's borders and that the end-time defeat of evil has already begun.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, many living among Gentiles, heard that no territory lies outside Jesus' rule, and that the powers they feared were already afraid of him.

traditions.q: Peter was married (8:14). May ordained ministers marry?
views: In the Latin Church, priests and bishops are normally chosen from men who promise lifelong celibacy "for the sake of the kingdom of heaven" (Catechism 1579; Code of Canon Law canon 277). This is a church discipline, not a doctrine: Eastern Catholic churches ordain married men as priests, and some married former Protestant ministers have been ordained. Bishops are always celibate.
A married man may be ordained deacon or priest, but a priest may not marry after ordination, and bishops are chosen from celibate monks, following canons of the late 600s.
The Augsburg Confession (article 23) defends the marriage of priests as God's order and a remedy against sin, and rejects compulsory celibacy as a human law.
"Bishops, Priests, and Deacons, are not commanded by God's Law" to vow single life, and may marry at their own discretion (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 32).

Ministers may marry. The Second Helvetic Confession (chapter 29) defends the marriage of ministers, the Westminster Confession rejects vows of perpetual single life as a snare (22.7), and Calvin called forced clerical celibacy a human law against God's word (Institutes 4.12.23–28).

traditions.q: Matthew applies Isaiah 53:4 to Jesus' healings (8:17). Is bodily healing provided in Christ's atonement, so that believers may claim it now?
views: Yes. Divine healing is part of the gospel: deliverance from sickness is provided for in the atonement and is the privilege of all believers (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, article 12, citing Isaiah 53:4–5 and Matthew 8:16–17).

Christ's passion is the source of all healing, and the Church continues his care in the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, which gives strength and peace and sometimes bodily healing if that serves the person's salvation (Catechism 1505, 1520). Jesus did not heal every sick person; his healings are signs of the kingdom.

Christ is the physician of soul and body. The church prays for healing in the service of Holy Unction and honors healings through the saints, but bodily healing is a gift of God's mercy, not a guaranteed right.

The atonement secures the resurrection of the body; it does not promise healing on demand now. Many in this tradition, following B. B. Warfield, hold that the miraculous healing gifts ended with the apostles, though God still heals in answer to prayer, and they read 8:17 as fulfilled in Jesus' earthly ministry.

Divided: Holiness and charismatic evangelicals, following A. B. Simpson, teach healing in the atonement; many other evangelicals hold that healing is one of the benefits of Christ's work fully received only at the resurrection.

title: Forgiving sinners, raising the dead
sum: Back in Capernaum, Jesus tells a paralyzed man that his sins are forgiven. Some scribes think he is blaspheming, so Jesus heals the man to show that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive. He calls Matthew from his tax booth and eats with tax collectors and sinners; to the Pharisees' complaint he answers with Hosea: "Mercy is what I want, not sacrifice." John's disciples ask why his followers do not fast, and he answers with pictures of a wedding, a patch and new wine.

Then come more deeds: an official's daughter raised from death, a woman healed of twelve years' bleeding when she touches the tassel of his cloak, two blind men who call him Son of David, and a man who could not speak. The crowds say nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel; the Pharisees say he works by the ruler of demons. The chapter ends with Jesus touring the towns, moved by the crowds who are like sheep without a shepherd, and telling his disciples to pray for workers for the harvest.
readings: Chapter 9 brings the first clashes with religious leaders: scribes (9:3), Pharisees (9:11, 34) and even John's disciples (9:14). The charges, blasphemy, eating with sinners, neglecting fasts, working with demonic power, are those that will return until the trial (26:65). Matthew shows the split forming: the crowds marvel, the leaders resist.

The chapter's key text is Hosea 6:6. Each scene shows mercy outranking a rule or a fear: a sinner forgiven, a tax collector called, a meal with outsiders, a woman who should not have touched him, blind men crying for mercy, shepherdless crowds. Jesus' compassion (9:36) drives what follows: the sending of the Twelve.

Every dispute here is about how to keep God's law faithfully: who may forgive, with whom one may eat, when to fast. These were live questions among Jews, and Jesus argues from the Prophets. Jewish scholars note that the rabbis too made Hosea 6:6 central after the Temple fell, so the argument is within Israel, not against it.

views.H: Toll collectors in Galilee served Herod Antipas's tax contracts. Funeral customs (flute players and wailing women), the tassels the Law required, purity rules for a woman with a discharge, and set days of fasting among pious Jews all fit first-century Galilee. That Jesus ate with notorious sinners, and was criticized for it, is one of the best-attested facts about him (11:19).
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 2:1–22 closely for the paralyzed man, the call, the meal and the fasting question, then Mark 5:21–43 for the daughter and the woman, cutting both sharply. The two blind men (9:27–31) and the man who could not speak (9:32–34) look like Matthew's own versions of stories he tells again later (20:29–34; 12:22–24), placed here to complete the ten miracles and to prepare for Jesus' answer to John in 11:5. He adds Hosea 6:6, which he uses twice.
views.L: The chapter shows the new and the old: new wine needs new skins, but "both are kept safe" (9:17). It also builds the title "Son of David" (9:27), which will grow through the Gospel, and the theme of faith (9:2, 22, 28–29). The closing summary (9:35) repeats 4:23 and closes the frame around chapters 5–9.
views.J: Jewish readers have pointed to rabbinic parallels: the Prayer of Nabonidus from Qumran, where a Jewish healer forgives sins; Yohanan ben Zakkai's use of Hosea 6:6 after AD 70; the Mishnah's funeral flute players. Amy-Jill Levine and others warn against sermons that make purity laws the villain of the bleeding woman's story: Matthew does not say so. The Pharisees here are the voice of Matthew's rivals after AD 70.
views.T: The fathers saw in the paralyzed man the soul paralyzed by sin, healed by forgiveness. The call of Matthew became a favorite subject of art (Caravaggio's Calling of Saint Matthew, 1600). The church's practice of fasting looked to 9:15: the bridegroom has been taken away, so Christians fast. Catholic and Orthodox teaching saw in 9:6–8 a forgiving authority given to the church's ministers.

deep.h: Jesus, the Law and the Pharisees in chapter 9
deep.b:
Three disputes, three different questions of law:

  • Forgiveness (9:2–8). No law forbade announcing forgiveness, but forgiveness was God's work, usually received through repentance and the sacrifices of the Temple. The scribes hear Jesus claiming God's own authority.
  • Table fellowship (9:10–13). The Torah does not forbid eating with sinners. The issue is the practice of pious groups, many of them Pharisees, who took care whom they ate with, and the general feeling that eating with the wicked approved of them. E. P. Sanders argued that Jesus' real offense was offering the kingdom to the wicked without first requiring the restitution the Law demanded.
  • Fasting (9:14–17). The Torah commands one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement. The Pharisees' twice-weekly fasts and the strict fasting of John's disciples were voluntary piety. Jesus does not reject fasting; he says it does not suit a wedding, and that it will return.

In each case Jesus argues from Scripture and from God's purpose, not by dismissing the Law. Matthew's readers, arguing with synagogue leaders of their own day, would have seen their debates in these.

Matthew uses two verbs for healing: therapeuō, "heal, care for" (from which "therapy") and sōzō, "save, rescue, make well." In the bleeding woman's story he uses sōzō three times in two verses (9:21–22). The Plain English Translation keeps "saved" there so the reader can hear the link with the name of Jesus, "save his people from their sins" (1:21). The paralyzed man shows the same link from the other side: forgiveness first, then healing. For Matthew, Jesus' healings are not side events but signs of the salvation he brings to the whole person, and promises of the resurrection that the raising of the official's daughter foreshadows.

settings.what: "Your sins are forgiven": the paralyzed man and the scribes
settings.to: a paralyzed man and the friends who carried him; then some scribes present, who object in their hearts; the crowds look on
settings.when: back in Capernaum, "his own town"
settings.why: Jesus speaks forgiveness first, then answers the scribes' unspoken charge by healing, so that the visible deed vouches for the invisible one. The words were meant to show the scribes and the crowd that the Son of Man has God's authority to forgive on earth.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, who forgave sins in Jesus' name (16:19; 18:18), heard the crowd's praise for authority given "to people" as a word about their own community.

settings.what: The call of Matthew and Jesus' answer about eating with sinners
settings.to: Matthew at the toll booth; then Pharisees who question his disciples at the meal
settings.when: at a meal in a house in Capernaum, crowded with tax collectors and sinners
settings.why: The rule at stake is not a law of the Torah but the custom of pious Jews, many of them Pharisees, who avoided eating with people known for breaking the Law. Jesus answers with a proverb (a doctor goes to the sick) and with Hosea 6:6: mercy matters more than ritual. He sends his critics back to their own Scriptures to learn.
settings.readers: In Matthew's day believers who welcomed Gentiles and sinners faced the same complaint from synagogue leaders, the heirs of the Pharisees; the scene gave them Jesus' answer.

settings.what: The question about fasting, and the parable of the groom's friends
settings.to: the disciples of John the Baptist
settings.when: soon after the meal with sinners
settings.why: John's disciples, devout and perhaps grieving their imprisoned teacher (4:12), ask why Jesus' followers skip the extra fasts that pious Jews kept. The Torah required only the fast of the Day of Atonement; these fasts were voluntary devotion. Jesus answers with a picture: guests do not mourn at a wedding. The time with the groom is a time of joy, though a day of loss is coming.
settings.readers: Matthew's church did fast (6:16–18; Didache 8:1), and 9:15 explained why: the groom had been taken away.

settings.what: The parable of the patch
settings.to: the disciples of John the Baptist, continuing his answer
settings.when: in the same conversation about fasting
settings.why: A second picture from daily life: a patch of new, unshrunk cloth tears an old garment worse. The newness Jesus brings cannot simply be stitched onto old habits of devotion.
settings.readers: Luke calls this saying a parable (Luke 5:36). For Matthew's readers it raised the question of how the new teaching fits with the old Law, which the next saying answers.

settings.what: The parable of the wine and the wineskins
settings.to: the disciples of John the Baptist, finishing his answer
settings.when: in the same conversation about fasting
settings.why: New wine still fermenting bursts old, stiff skins, so it needs new ones. Only Matthew adds the final words: "both are kept safe."
settings.readers: Matthew's Jewish-Christian readers, holding on to the Law while following Jesus, heard that new and old need not be lost.
views: The images show that the gospel cannot be contained in Judaism (a reading common in later Christianity, at its extreme in Marcion).
Matthew's "both are kept safe" means the new teaching and the old Law are both preserved (many modern commentators).

settings.what: The official's plea, the woman's touch, and Jesus' words to the mourners
settings.by: the official, the woman (to herself), then Jesus
settings.to: Jesus; then the woman; then the flute players and the crowd in the official's house
settings.when: while Jesus is still answering John's disciples, on the way to the official's house
settings.why: The father asks for the impossible, life for a daughter already dead. The woman, whose bleeding made her ritually unclean, speaks only to herself, hoping a touch of his tassel will be enough. Jesus calls her "daughter" and names her faith; then he tells the mourners the girl is only sleeping, and they laugh. His words show that faith is met even when it is quiet, and that death is not final in his presence.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers, who buried their own dead, heard death called sleep, as Christians soon called it (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14).

settings.what: The two blind men and Jesus' question about faith
settings.to: Jesus; then the two blind men
settings.when: as Jesus leaves the official's house, and then inside a house
settings.why: The men shout "Son of David," a royal title, in public. Jesus waits until they are indoors, asks whether they believe he can do this, and heals them "as you have believed." His stern order to tell no one fits his wish not to be hailed as a political king.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers knew Jesus as the Son of David (1:1); the scene taught that the title belongs to a healer, not a warlord.

settings.what: The crowds' amazement and the Pharisees' charge
settings.to: each other, about Jesus
settings.when: after Jesus throws out a demon from a man who could not speak
settings.why: Two verdicts close the chapters of deeds: the crowds say "Nothing like this has ever appeared in Israel," while the Pharisees say Jesus works with the ruler of the demons. The split prepares for the mission speech, where Jesus warns that his messengers will be called the same names (10:25).
settings.readers: Matthew's readers heard the same charge against their Lord from their opponents, and so knew they should expect it for themselves.

settings.what: The harvest and the workers
settings.to: his disciples
settings.when: while touring Galilee's towns, moved by the crowds
settings.why: To turn the disciples' eyes to the crowds' need and to teach them to pray for workers. The prayer prepares them to become the answer: in the next verse Jesus sends them.
settings.readers: Matthew's community, still sending missionaries (10:5–42; 28:19), prayed this prayer for its own workers.

traditions.q: The crowd praises God for giving authority to forgive sins "to people" (9:8). Can a minister of the church declare God's forgiveness with Christ's authority?
views: Yes. Christ gave his apostles, and through them bishops and priests, the power to forgive sins; in the sacrament of Penance the priest absolves the penitent in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Catechism 1441–1442, 1461).

Yes. In the mystery of Confession the priest stands as a witness beside the penitent before Christ; the prayer of absolution asks God's forgiveness and declares it by the grace given to the priesthood.

Yes. Private confession and absolution are kept, and the absolution spoken by the pastor is to be received as God's own word of forgiveness (Augsburg Confession, articles 11 and 25; Small Catechism, on Confession).

The Book of Common Prayer gives a general absolution in worship, and in the Visitation of the Sick a priest may absolve a penitent "by his authority committed to me"; private confession is available but not required.

Forgiveness is declared to believers through the preaching of the gospel and exercised through church discipline, the "keys of the kingdom" (Heidelberg Catechism 83–85); there is no sacrament of penance and no priestly absolution.

Only God forgives sins. Believers confess to God directly through Christ, the one mediator, and to one another for healing and accountability; a pastor can assure them of God's promise but does not absolve.

title: Sheep among wolves: the mission discourse
sum: Jesus gives his twelve disciples authority over unclean spirits and disease, and Matthew lists their names. Then comes the second of the five great speeches in Matthew. Jesus sends the Twelve only to "the sheep of the house of Israel that are lost," not to Gentiles or Samaritans. They are to announce that the kingdom of heaven has drawn near and to do what he has done: heal, raise the dead, cleanse, drive out demons, all for free. They go without money or spare clothes, living on the welcome of worthy households, and shake the dust off their feet where they are refused.

The speech then looks past that first trip. The messengers will be sheep among wolves: flogged in synagogues, brought before governors and kings, betrayed by their families, hated by all. The Spirit of their Father will give them words; whoever holds out to the end will be saved; and they will not finish the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. They are not to fear those who kill only the body, for the Father counts every hair. Jesus brings not peace but a sword, and following him means taking up a cross. But anyone who welcomes them welcomes him, and even a cup of cold water given to one of these little ones will be rewarded.
readings: Read as a charge to the Twelve

On its face the speech is Jesus' briefing before a short preaching tour of Galilee's Jewish towns. The rules about travel, greeting, lodging and leaving fit that trip, and the limit to Israel fits Jesus' own mission (15:24). Matthew does not say the Twelve went or came back, which suggests he cares more about the instructions than the trip.
Read as a charge to the church

From 10:17 on the speech reaches into a future of synagogue courts, governors, kings and the Gentiles, the experience of Jesus' followers after the resurrection. Most scholars think Matthew gathered sayings from Mark 6, Mark 13 and the sayings source shared with Luke into one speech for his own church's missionaries, so that every generation of messengers hears Jesus' charge.
Read as the disciples sharing Jesus' story

Everything the disciples are told to do or suffer, Jesus has done or will suffer: authority, healing, homelessness, rejection, the charge of working with Beelzebul, betrayal, being handed over, the cross. "A disciple does not rank above the teacher" (10:24): the apostles' life is to copy their Lord's.

views.H: Wandering preachers who lived on hospitality were familiar in Jesus' world, and Galilee's villages were close together. Jewish local courts could flog members of the synagogue, and Galileans knew Roman crucifixion all too well. That Jesus chose a group of twelve as a sign for Israel's tribes is widely accepted as historical, even by critical scholars such as E. P. Sanders and John P. Meier. Whether he also forbade a mission to Gentiles and Samaritans (10:5–6) is much more debated: some think the saying is his and explains why the later Gentile mission needed the risen Lord's command (28:19); others think it comes from a strict group of Jewish believers in Matthew's tradition.
views.C: Matthew builds the speech from Mark 6:7–13 (the sending), Mark 13:9–13 (persecution, moved here from Jesus' speech about the end), and material shared with Luke (Luke 10:2–16; Luke 12:2–12, 51–53; Luke 14:26–27). The Israel-only command (10:5–6) and the saying about the Son of Man coming (10:23) are found only in Matthew. Critics debate whether they come from early Jewish-Christian missionaries or from Jesus himself.
views.L: This is the second discourse, ending with Matthew's formula "When Jesus had finished..." (11:1). It moves from the near mission (10:5–15) to the long future (10:16–23), to comfort and warning (10:24–33), to the cost (10:34–39), and ends with reward (10:40–42). Key words repeat: "worthy" (10:10–13, 37–38), "hand over" (10:4, 17, 19, 21), "do not fear" (10:26, 28, 31), "take in" (10:40–41).
views.J: The mission is entirely to Israel, and the persecution described is a quarrel within Israel: synagogue courts discipline their own members. Jewish scholars note that the speech's language (the agent who is like the sender, "go and learn," Micah 7:6 as a sign of the Messiah's coming) is Jewish through and through. Matthew's "their synagogues" (10:17) reflects his community's separation, not the attitude of Jesus and the Twelve.
views.T: Church history is full of attempts to live 10:9–10 literally: the desert monks, Francis of Assisi (who, about 1208, heard the Gospel of the sending of the disciples read at Mass and changed his life), the Waldensians, and Anabaptist preachers. The martyrs drew courage from 10:28 and 10:32–33. Catholic tradition reads the list headed by "first, Simon" as a sign of Peter's primacy; Protestant readers see him as first among equals.

deep.h: The shape of the mission discourse
deep.b:
• The sending (10:1–4): authority given; the twelve names.
  • Instructions for the road (10:5–15): to Israel only; the message and the deeds; no money; lodging; peace; shaking off the dust.
  • Sheep among wolves (10:16–23): courts, synagogues, governors; the Spirit's help; family betrayal; enduring; fleeing; the Son of Man's coming.
  • Do not fear (10:24–33): like the teacher; all will be revealed; fear God, not killers; sparrows and hairs; confessing and denying.
  • Not peace but a sword (10:34–39): division in families; worthiness; the cross; losing and finding life.
  • Welcome and reward (10:40–42): receiving the messengers is receiving Jesus and God.

Notice how the speech widens: from a tour of Galilean villages to governors, kings and the Gentiles (10:18) and the end of the age (10:22–23).

Few verses have caused more debate. Jesus says the messengers will not finish the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. Five main readings:

  1. A mistaken expectation. Albert Schweitzer built his picture of Jesus on this verse: Jesus expected the end to come before the Twelve returned, and when it did not, he went to Jerusalem to force it. Few now follow Schweitzer's whole theory, but some critical scholars think the saying reflects an early Christian hope that was not fulfilled in the way expected.
  2. The resurrection or Pentecost. The Son of Man "comes" in vindication when he is raised and given all authority (28:18), soon after.
  3. The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. R. T. France and preterist readers link it to Daniel 7:13 as a coming to the throne, seen in the judgment on the Temple within a generation (compare 24:34).
  4. The second coming, with Israel's mission continuing. The mission to the Jewish people will not be complete before Jesus returns; the verse is a promise that Israel will not be abandoned, as Paul hopes (Romans 11:25–26).
  5. A future tribulation witness. Many dispensationalists read the discourse as also describing a Jewish witness during a future tribulation before Christ's return.

Matthew placed the saying in a speech that runs to the end of the age, so for his readers it promised that their dangerous mission would end in the Son of Man's coming.

deep.title: Claude's theory: chapter 10 retells chapters 8–9 for the disciples
deep.b:
My suggestion is that Matthew built the mission discourse as a mirror of the ten miracles. Each part of the disciples' charge repeats something Jesus has just lived through in chapters 8–9:

  • Authority given (10:1) answers the authority God gave "to people" (9:8).
  • The list of deeds (10:8) matches the miracles in order of their first appearance: healing (8:5–17), raising (9:18–26), cleansing (8:1–4), exorcism (8:28–34).
  • No bag, no home (10:9–11) answers "the Son of Man does not have anywhere to rest his head" (8:20).
  • Towns that refuse them (10:14) recall the town that asked Jesus to leave (8:34).
  • Called Beelzebul (10:25) answers the Pharisees' charge (9:34).
  • Family set at odds (10:35–37) answers "Let the dead bury their own dead" (8:22).
  • Sheep and harvest (10:6, 16) pick up 9:36–38.

If so, Matthew wants readers to see the church's mission as Jesus' own story lived again. The link between 10:8 and chapters 8–9, and between 10:25 and 9:34, is widely noted (for example by Davies and Allison); the full mirror is my proposal.

settings.what: The mission discourse, the second of Matthew's five great speeches
settings.to: the Twelve, just named (10:1–5), sent to the towns of Israel
settings.when: during Jesus' Galilean ministry, after his tour of the towns (9:35) and his call to pray for workers (9:38)
settings.why: To send the Twelve out with his authority and his message, to tell them how to travel and whom to approach, and to prepare them for rejection, persecution and division without fear. The speech makes them extensions of Jesus himself: whoever receives them receives him.
settings.readers: Matthew's community, decades later, still sent out preachers and suffered at the hands of synagogue courts and Roman officials. Matthew shaped the speech so that its later sections speak directly to them, and it ends with the promise that even the smallest kindness to a messenger counts.
views: Traditional readers take the discourse as one charge given by Jesus at one time, including prophecies of the later mission.
Most critical scholars think Matthew combined sayings from Mark 6, Mark 13 and the sayings source shared with Luke into one speech for his own church.
Luke gives a short charge to the Twelve (Luke 9:1–6), a longer one to seventy-two others (Luke 10:1–16), and the persecution and fear sayings in other settings (Luke 12; Luke 21).

settings.what: Rules for the road
settings.to: the Twelve, before their first journey
settings.when: as he sends them out
settings.why: These are travel rules for this mission: whom to visit (Israel only), what to say and do, what not to carry, where to stay and what to do when refused. They bind the Twelve on this journey, in the villages of Galilee and the land of Israel. Traveling with nothing meant total trust in God and in the hospitality of Israel's households, and made the messengers look like their message: a free gift.
settings.readers: Early churches adapted these rules (Luke 22:35–36 shows Jesus himself changing them; the Didache sets limits on traveling prophets). Later movements, from Francis of Assisi to Anabaptist preachers, took them literally.
views: Many readers hold the rules applied to the Twelve's Galilean mission and were changed later (Luke 22:35–36).
Others see a lasting model of simplicity and dependence for every preacher of the gospel.

settings.what: Sheep among wolves
settings.to: the Twelve
settings.when: within the mission speech
settings.why: To warn them that rejection will come from courts, synagogues, rulers and even families, and to give them three supports: the Spirit's words, the promise to the one who endures, and the coming of the Son of Man. Knowing the danger in advance keeps them from being shaken by it.
settings.readers: The words reached later messengers too. For Matthew's readers this was already history: flogging in synagogues, trials before governors and kings (Acts), believers betrayed by relatives. The section assured them that Jesus had foreseen it.

settings.what: Do not be afraid
settings.to: the Twelve
settings.when: within the mission speech
settings.why: Three times he says "do not fear": the truth will come out; human killers cannot touch the soul; the Father cares for every sparrow and counts every hair. The fear of God drives out the fear of people, and the promise that Jesus will acknowledge them before the Father gives courage to acknowledge him before people.
settings.readers: Christians on trial, who might save their lives by denying Christ, heard 10:32–33 as the choice before them.

settings.what: Not peace but a sword
settings.to: the Twelve
settings.when: within the mission speech
settings.why: To make plain that loyalty to him will split families, as Micah 7:6 foretold of the last days, and that he must come before father, mother, son and daughter. The words prepare the messengers for division in their own homes and in the homes they visit.
settings.readers: Jewish believers in Matthew's community often lost family ties by following Jesus; the sayings told them this was the expected cost, not a sign of failure.

settings.what: Whoever takes you in
settings.to: the Twelve
settings.when: at the close of the mission speech
settings.why: To end with reward: messengers carry Jesus' presence, so households that welcome them welcome him and God. Even a cup of cold water given to a humble disciple will not go unrewarded.
settings.readers: Matthew's church depended on hospitality to traveling prophets and teachers; this told the hosts who welcomed them that their kindness was service to Christ.

traditions.q: Jesus sends the Twelve to heal the sick and raise the dead (10:8). Do the gifts of healing and miracles continue in the church today?
views: Yes. The gifts of the Spirit, including healing and miracles, belong to the church in every age until Christ returns, and believers should seek them (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, articles 7 and 12).

Yes. The Holy Spirit still gives charisms, including healing, for the good of the Church, to be tested by the Church's pastors (Catechism 798–801); the Church examines reported miracles, for example in causes for sainthood.
Yes. Miracles continue in the life of the church, especially through the saints, their relics and the holy icons, as signs of God's presence rather than proofs on demand.

Many hold that the miraculous sign gifts ceased with the apostles, whose message they confirmed, though God still answers prayer for healing (B. B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles). Some Reformed churches and teachers are continuationist.

A general description: evangelicals are divided between cessationists, who hold that the apostolic sign gifts ended, and continuationists, including the wider charismatic movement, who expect all the gifts today.

traditions.q: Jesus speaks of God destroying "soul and body alike in Gehenna" (10:28). Does this mean everlasting punishment, or that the lost will cease to exist?
views: Hell is eternal: the souls of those who die in mortal sin suffer the punishments of hell, chiefly eternal separation from God; the soul is immortal (Catechism 1033–1035).

Punishment is eternal. Many Orthodox teachers describe hell as experiencing God's love as torment by those who refuse it; some fathers, such as Gregory of Nyssa, hoped for the restoration of all, a view never made dogma.
The wicked will be cast into eternal torments and punished with everlasting destruction (Westminster Confession 33.2).
The soul is not naturally immortal. The wicked will be destroyed by fire at the end, not tormented forever; "destroy" here means just that (Fundamental Beliefs).
There is no hell of fire; Gehenna is a symbol of everlasting destruction, from which there is no resurrection.
Most hold to eternal conscious punishment; a growing minority, including John Stott tentatively and Edward Fudge, hold that the lost are finally destroyed (conditional immortality).

traditions.q: "Whoever holds out to the end, that person will be saved" (10:22). Can a true believer fall away and be lost?
views: Yes. Grace can be lost through mortal sin and restored through the sacrament of Penance. Final perseverance is a special gift of God, and no one can be absolutely certain of it without a special revelation (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 13 and canon 16; Catechism 1861).
Yes. Salvation is a lifelong path of union with God, and a believer can turn away from it; the saying is a call to keep struggling to the end.

Yes. The Augsburg Confession (article 12) rejects the view that those once justified cannot lose the Holy Spirit; those who fall can be restored through repentance. Yet God's election of his own is sure and gives comfort (Formula of Concord, article 11).

No. Those whom God has called and sanctified "can neither totally nor finally fall away" but will persevere to the end and be saved (Westminster Confession 17.1). Holding out to the end is the mark of true faith, and God keeps those who are his.
Yes. John Wesley argued that a true believer can make shipwreck of faith and perish, so the warnings to endure are real (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints, 1751).

Most Baptist confessions teach that all true believers endure to the end and will never fall away finally (Baptist Faith and Message, article 5; Second London Confession, chapter 17). General (Free Will) Baptists teach that a believer can fall away.
